extracted.intended_audience: general readers, journalists, and legal practitioners interested in UK privacy and media law
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts the legal standards and evaluative criteria applied in the High Court privacy/breach-of-confidence case Mosley v News Group Newspapers Ltd (2008), used to assess whether publication of private information was unlawful and what remedies were appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonable expectation of privacy
rubrics_metrics.description: The first hurdle was the need to show a reasonable expectation of privacy; the law now affords protection to information in respect of which there is a reasonable expectation of privacy, even in circumstances where there is no preexisting relationship giving rise of itself to an enforceable duty of confidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Justice Eady stated this following the Human Rights Act 1998 and authorities such as Campbell v MGN Ltd. If a claimant can show a reasonable expectation of privacy, the court then weighs competing Convention rights (Article 8 v Article 10).

rubrics_metrics.name: Breach of confidence by conduct inconsistent with a pre-existing relationship
rubrics_metrics.description: Breach of confidence can arise 'by way of conduct inconsistent with a pre-existing relationship, rather than simply of the purloining of private information' (authority: McKennitt v Ash).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mosley's claim relied in part on this principle: liability may arise from conduct that violates an expectation of confidentiality even where the breach is not a straightforward theft of documents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balancing Articles 8 and 10 (privacy v freedom of expression)
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a reasonable expectation of privacy is established, it is then a matter of weighing up the competing Convention rights — the claimant's Article 8 rights against the defendant's Article 10 rights (freedom of expression).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The court applies proportionality and public interest analysis (drawing on cases like Campbell). A defendant must show a genuine public interest to justify publication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public interest exception (when sexual conduct becomes public interest)
rubrics_metrics.description: Sadomasochistic behaviour is generally not a matter of public interest, but there could be a public interest if the behaviour involved the mocking of Jews or the Holocaust.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The judgment makes clear that ordinary private sexual conduct (including adultery or BDSM) does not automatically become justifiable to publish unless there is an accompanying public-interest element (e.g., behaviour mocking victims of the Holocaust). In Mosley the court found no such public-interest element.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement of particularized evidence for asserted Nazi element
rubrics_metrics.description: The court required evidence that the gathering was intended as an enactment of Nazi behaviour; mere German-themed props or accents were insufficient to prove a 'Nazi' element.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Justice Eady found equating 'everything German with Nazism' offensive and concluded that items cited (Luftwaffe jacket, striped uniforms, shaved heads, German-sounding speech) did not show anything specific to the Nazi period. The presence or absence of a Nazi element materially affected the public-interest balancing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Availability of injunction — effectiveness and futility
rubrics_metrics.description: An injunction may be refused if the material is already too widely available for the injunction to serve any purpose; widespread availability undermines the remedy's utility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mosley's initial application for an injunction to prevent republication was denied because the video was too widely available; subsequently a permanent injunction was granted restraining the newspaper from showing the video, illustrating that availability and practical effectiveness are key factors in injunctive relief.

rubrics_metrics.name: Damages for invasion of privacy
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts may award monetary damages for unlawful publication of private information; in this case Mosley was awarded £60,000.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The size of damages can influence media behaviour and prompt commentary about chilling effects on investigative journalism; commentators debate whether damages levels will deter lawful publication when public interest exists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allegation of criminality is distinct and must be established
rubrics_metrics.description: Allegations that private conduct amounted to a crime (e.g., under the Offences against the Person Act 1861) must be established; Justice Eady rejected the argument that Mosley could be said to have committed a crime on himself under that Act.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criminality allegations may be used by defendants to justify publication, but they require their own legal basis and proof and are treated separately from privacy/confidence claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weight and credibility of evidence (deleted emails, witness testimony, payments)
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts assess the reliability and weight of evidence such as deleted e-mails, witness testimony, and payments to participants; the News of the World relied on deleted e-mails and the conduct of witnesses, while one witness (Woman E) who recorded the incident was later not relied upon.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Issues like deletion of material, payments to witnesses (£20,000 to Woman E), and changing witness positions affect credibility and the court's factual findings about what occurred and whether the public interest defence is made out.

rubrics_metrics.name: Human Rights Act 1998 effect on privacy protection
rubrics_metrics.description: The Human Rights Act 1998 requires that domestic law give effect to Convention rights; it led the court to conclude that protection is afforded to information where there is a reasonable expectation of privacy, even absent a pre-existing duty of confidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: HRA incorporation means Articles 8 and 10 are central to domestic privacy/confidence disputes; courts apply ECHR principles when balancing rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between privacy/confidence claims and defamation/libel claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Mosley relied upon breach of confidence/unauthorised disclosure of personal information rather than defamation; libel is a separate cause of action (a libel action was later brought).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claimants choose the appropriate legal route depending on whether the complaint is that false statements harmed reputation (defamation) or that private information was unlawfully published (privacy/breach of confidence). Remedies and defences differ.

rubrics_metrics.name: Application to Strasbourg / margin of appreciation and effective remedy (Articles 8 and 13)
rubrics_metrics.description: An application to the European Court of Human Rights raised whether the UK's failure to legislate to require pre-publication warning amounted to breach of Articles 8 and 13; the ECtHR ruled against Mosley, finding a state's margin of appreciation in deciding whether to legislate on that matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Domestic judgments can be challenged at Strasbourg, but the ECtHR gives states some discretion (margin of appreciation) on how to regulate press/private-life conflicts; Article 13 (effective remedy) claims require showing inadequate domestic remedies.
